title: Thanks in all things (1 Thessalonians 5:18)
hook: not for everything, but in everything

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph naming the evil, and God at work in the same chapter. Your line was every chapter held.

A hospital waiting room in the middle of the night. Bad coffee, a television nobody watches, a phone almost dead. On the table, someone has left a card with a sunrise on it: give thanks in all things. It can land like a slap. Thanks for this? For the scan, the layoff, the empty chair? But the line is older than the card, from a letter Paul wrote to the church in Thessalonica, and read slowly, it doesn't say what the card seems to say. One small word carries it.
screen: `A CARD WITH A SUNRISE ON IT.`

segments.voice: Near the letter's end, Paul fires off short lines like notes on a fridge. In the King James words: "Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you." In every thing. Not for every thing. Some readers put it this way: the hard thing is a room, and thanks is something said inside it. Nobody is asked to call the diagnosis a gift. The thanks is for what's still true in there: a nurse who brings a blanket, a friend who answers at midnight, the breath you're still taking. Another letter, Ephesians, speaks of "giving thanks always for all things." Christians read that in more than one way. Some hear trust that God can bring good even out of what hurts. Others hear thanks for every good gift, offered at all times. Scripture doesn't hand over one tidy rule; the two lines sit side by side. Then there's Job. In one day he hears that his animals, his servants and his children are gone. He tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground, and worships: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Look at the order. The torn robe comes first. The grief isn't skipped to get to the blessing. Both happen on the same ground, the same day. That's the shape of in, not for. The tears stay, and somewhere in the room, one good thing gets named.
screen: `IN, NOT FOR: THANKS INSIDE THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that's hard right now, and let it be as heavy as it is. Still inside it, look for one true good, a person who stayed, a warm cup, a text that came at the right time, and hold it; you don't need to be grateful for the hard thing itself. If you pray, thank God for that good in your own words; if not, let a quiet thank you rest on it.
Thanks in all things. Paul's line to the Thessalonians: in every thing give thanks. Thanks said inside the hard moment, without calling the hard moment good.
Your line: in, not for. One small word makes all the difference. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians give thanks in prayers at meals, at bedtime and in church services, and a Christian funeral may give thanks for a life even while people grieve.
